# A Map of AI-for-Architecture Work {#sec-appendix-b-ai-for-architecture-map}

::: {.abstract}
This appendix consolidates the prior body of AI-for-architecture work that Architecture 2.0 builds on. It groups established results into families, maps each family to the principal lifecycle stages where cited work demonstrates activity, and shows how the discipline of an AI-native design system differs from any single method family. This map serves as a positioning statement rather than an exhaustive literature survey.
:::

Machine learning has appeared in computer architecture for decades. Early work proposed learned in-chip mechanisms and models of architectural design spaces. More recent systems couple learned methods directly to simulators, compilers, and implementation tools. The families below form the foundation on which this work builds; because existing literature already provides comprehensive surveys [@ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture], this appendix offers a positioning aid instead (@tbl-ai-arch-map).

When examined by their underlying claims, most method families fall into three regimes, with each regime supporting a distinct claim. Learned in-chip components occupy the mechanism regime, evaluated against the mechanism's own budget, such as mispredict rate at fixed storage and latency. Learned cost models occupy the design-space-model regime, evaluated by their predictive fidelity against the tool they approximate. Families that participate in the design process itself occupy the third regime. Benchmarks and datasets sit alongside these regimes as supporting evaluation infrastructure. A complete third-regime result must be judged at the level of the architecture study rather than by the generated artifact alone. Confusing these regimes allows a bounded branch-prediction result to be mistaken for evidence that an agent can be trusted with a floorplan.

| **Family of work** | **Representative results** | **Principal lifecycle stages demonstrated** | **Developed in** | **Key sources** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Learned in-chip components** | Perceptron branch predictors and learned prefetchers, where learning is embedded in the mechanism itself and does a bounded tactical job | Implement, Evaluate | @sec-moonshot, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron; @ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture] |
| **Learned cost models and predictive DSE** | Surrogates and regression models that predict performance and power across a Design Space Exploration (DSE) environment from cheap features | Explore, Evaluate | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] |

: **The unit of work in Architecture 2.0 is the architecture study and its reviewable claim, not any single family's artifact.** Each row names prior results, the principal lifecycle stages demonstrated by the cited work, and the chapters that develop it. The stage column uses only the six labels defined in @sec-architecture-20-ontology. {#tbl-ai-arch-map tbl-colwidths="[18,32,16,16,18]"}

These families are not mutually exclusive. An agentic design-space search might call a learned cost model, invoke an autoscheduler, and emit RTL within a single study touching several rows at once.

The learned in-chip components family carries a constraint that the others do not. A proposed component is only useful when its inference fits the mechanism's storage and latency budget. The perceptron predictor provides a bounded example, keeping within a 4\ KB hardware budget and delivering a prediction in one cycle [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron]. This result ties predictive accuracy directly to the hardware resources consumed inside the mechanism.

These families also occupy distinct regions of the territory mapped in @fig-book-composition. The learned-components, cost-model, and autotuning families live where computer architecture meets machine learning. Reinforcement learning for physical design and LLM-driven RTL generation live where machine learning meets electronic design automation (EDA). Learned models can use earlier-stage features to predict routing hotspots and downstream-flow outcomes [@Kahng2018Machine]. These surrogates extend the cost-model family into physical design, where a fast prediction guides iteration before running an expensive downstream flow. Generated assertions and testbenches span both regions, but they remain candidate verification collateral requiring independent execution and review [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM; @QiuEtAl2024AutoBench; @KangEtAl2024FVEval]. AgentDSE places tool feedback inside exploration, while QuArch contributes an Evaluate-stage test of architecture knowledge and question answering.

The stage column in @tbl-ai-arch-map carries a telling asymmetry: Explore appears in four rows, Implement in six, and Evaluate in six, yet no row demonstrates Formulate, Interpret and Explain, or Review and Decide. A complete architecture study must supply those missing responsibilities.

Because architecture studies often combine these methods, what separates Architecture 2.0 from any single family is the unit of work. A learned branch predictor changes a single mechanism. A macro-placement agent proposes a candidate for one implementation step. An RTL-generating model produces a single artifact. Prior literature judges each result on that bounded output alone.

Architecture 2.0 takes the complete architecture study and its reviewable claim as the fundamental unit of work. For architects, the question is not whether a model produced a plausible artifact, but whether the complete loop supports an architectural decision that another architect can inspect, reproduce, and challenge. The families mapped here supply the methods; the discipline of Architecture 2.0 supplies the standard of judgment that decides what their outputs actually support.

## The Latent Architectural Space Map

A central theme across Architecture 2.0 is that machine learning models do not operate directly on raw physical silicon. Instead, they transform complex, discrete, high-dimensional hardware artifacts (such as Abstract Syntax Trees, Control-Data Flow Graphs, place-and-route netlists, and memory trace logs) into continuous or structured latent space representations. Evaluating how different representation paradigms construct, navigate, and decode these latent spaces determines their resolving power and failure modes (@tbl-latent-space-map).

Four paradigms organize this territory: Token & Code Embeddings, Graph & Topological Embeddings, Continuous Surrogate & DSE Spaces, and Policy & Reinforcement State Spaces. Whatever the paradigm, a candidate latent point earns trust only through an independent physical grounding path, and each paradigm fails in its own way when its predictions diverge from physical hardware behavior.

| **Latent Space Paradigm** | **Underlying Representation** | **Search & Inference Mechanism** | **Physical Grounding & Decoupling** | **Primary Latent Failure Mode** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Token & Code Embeddings** | High-dimensional dense vectors derived from Large Language Model (LLM) Transformer activations over Verilog, SystemC, or Triton DSL code | Autoregressive token sampling, temperature decoding, and beam search | Executable compilation via Verilator or Yosys and functional testbenches | **Hallucinated Syntax & Vacuous Syntax:** Generated code looks syntactically plausible but violates ABI, bit-width, or structural invariants. |
| **Graph & Topological Embeddings** | Node and edge embeddings (Graph Neural Networks / GNNs, Hypergraphs) capturing spatial connectivity, CDFGs, or netlist floorplans | Node classification, edge prediction, and spatial clustering | Physical place-and-route tools via OpenROAD or Synopsys Innovus and static timing analyzers via OpenSTA | **Non-Routable Clustering:** Surrogates cluster macros optimally in graph space, but extracted physical layouts collapse under severe metal layer congestion. |
| **Continuous Surrogate & DSE Spaces** | Low-dimensional continuous manifolds mapping discrete architecture configurations (cache size, pipeline depth, bus width) to scalar PPA estimates | Bayesian Optimization (BO), Gaussian Processes, and active learning acquisition functions | Cycle-accurate simulators like SCALE-Sim or gem5 and gate-level signoff via Ansys RedHawk-SC | **Out-of-Distribution Exploitation (Optimizer's Curse):** Optimizers select extreme latent points whose predicted gains are inflated by estimation error rather than by real PPA improvements [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. |
| **Policy & Reinforcement State Spaces** | Markov Decision Process (MDP) state-action vectors representing placement steps, tile schedules, or circuit transformations | Deep Q-Networks (DQN), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) | Downstream physical DRC/LVS signoff and formal property checkers via Cadence JasperGold | **Reward Hacking:** The policy maximizes proxy reward functions (e.g., estimated wirelength) by injecting false timing paths or unfeasible constraints. |

: **Mapping latent architectural spaces across representation paradigms.** Each paradigm embeds discrete hardware artifacts into continuous or graph-based latent vectors. Physical grounding through independent signoff engines remains mandatory to prevent latent hallucinations from reaching silicon. {#tbl-latent-space-map tbl-colwidths="[18,22,18,20,22]"}

Mapping learned methods to their underlying latent space paradigms clarifies the evidence required to validate a candidate design. A model operating in token space establishes code syntax; validating its hardware claim requires decoding that token sequence into RTL and evaluating it through physical synthesis and static timing signoff.

These four latent paradigms (token vectors, topological graphs, continuous manifolds, and policy MDP state-action pairs) meet physical reality through a fundamental structural decoupling, separating latent candidate generation above from physical silicon signoff below (@fig-latent-architectural-space-map). To prevent latent failure modes (vacuous syntax, non-routable metal congestion, optimizer exploitation, and reward hacking) from corrupting the design loop, candidate proposals must pass through an independent, evaluator-owned physical grounding funnel. This funnel forces proposals through deterministic simulation, formal property verification, place-and-route netlists, and static timing signoff, ensuring that only physically grounded candidates receive approval from the human commitment authority before tapeout freeze.

![**The Latent Architectural Space Map decouples latent candidate generation from physical silicon signoff.** Machine learning models operate over four core representation paradigms (Token & Code Embeddings, Graph & Topological Embeddings, Continuous Surrogates, and Policy State Spaces). Each paradigm relies on an independent, evaluator-owned physical grounding path (Verilator, OpenROAD, SCALE-Sim, JasperGold) to prevent latent failure modes (Vacuous Syntax, Non-Routable Congestion, Optimizer's Curse, Reward Hacking) from reaching silicon. Verified candidates require human architect and commitment authority signoff across five clean physical signoff checks before tapeout freeze.](images/fig-latent-architectural-space-map){#fig-latent-architectural-space-map width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture diagram showing 4 Latent Space Paradigms at top, an Independent Evaluator-Owned Physical Signoff Barrier in the middle, and Verified Physical Silicon Signoff with Human Architect Commitment Authority at bottom."}

## Candidates, Not Decisions

In an AI-native design system, model outputs are always candidates, never final decisions. An autoscheduler's proposed schedule supports a performance claim only after measured execution on target hardware. A proposed placement requires downstream place-and-route, timing, power, and congestion checks. Generated RTL requires functional and implementation checks. The accountable organization retains commitment authority, while verification and implementation owners retain signoff authority for their respective domains.

Candidates can mislead through false confidence or hidden total costs. Generated assertions can pass vacuously while checking nothing that actually matters, meaning apparent success is not independent evidence [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity; @Clarke2018ModelChecking] (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). When evaluating macro-placement methods such as AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], a fair total-cost comparison must include the pretraining and fine-tuning runs actually used for the reported design, together with their compute [@ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. Neither apparent verification success nor a favorable cost comparison replaces the required domain signoff and organizational commitment.

## Survey of Existing AI-Assisted Systems

Public examples through July 2026 demonstrate individual point capabilities rather than a complete end-to-end design system. Their strongest claims become clearer when the checks behind each result are made explicit. For each system, architects must ask what artifact it produced, what test could reject it, how much of the broader architecture problem that test actually observes, and what can be inspected from the outside. Following those checks reveals both real progress and remaining gaps, without mistakenly treating fundamentally different systems as steps in a single ranking.

Exact or inexpensive checks support strong claims over a narrow task. For example, AlphaTensor found a 4 by 4 matrix-multiplication algorithm for a two-element domain that uses 47 scalar multiplications rather than Strassen's 49 [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor]. Because every candidate admitted an exact algebraic check, the system could confidently accept or reject solutions. Similarly, AutoTVM evaluates many tensor-program schedules on real hardware; the result is measured directly, and most failures stay contained inside the tuning run [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. While these reliable checks make search practical, neither result produces a complete system architecture.

Relying on proxy and simulator feedback enables broader exploration, but inherits the limits of the checking models. AlphaChip uses wirelength and congestion proxies to guide macro placement [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. ArchGym demonstrated that no single search algorithm dominates across design spaces when simulators and sample budgets are held fixed [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. To reduce costly target evaluations, Apollo transfers knowledge across related accelerator design spaces, whereas BOOM-Explorer pays hours per sample to execute a documented 7\ nm flow [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]. Each result is meaningful within its chosen feedback source, yet requires stronger evidence before supporting a wider physical or system claim.

Functional tests, post-synthesis metrics, and fabricated silicon establish vastly different levels of hardware progress. Because functional success alone cannot guarantee hardware design quality, VerilogEval focuses on functional simulation [@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval], while RTLLM layers on post-synthesis design-quality measures, though still stopping short of physical signoff [@RTLLM]. Pushing further, Chip-Chat reached tapeout for a small processor through extensive human-guided revision, and Enlightenment-1 produced a fabricated RISC-V core by expanding Boolean-function representations from input-output examples, an approach framed as eliminating the manual verify-and-debug loop [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat; @ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU]. These represent significant implementation achievements, yet neither system delivers the full multi-tool system-architecture capability that the moonshot poses.

Human ratings and proprietary deployment reports remain much harder to evaluate from the outside. ChipNeMo reports task-specific internal gains, ChatEDA checks tool execution alongside human-rated request fulfillment, and DSO.ai announces 100 commercial tapeouts without a public matched methodology [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA; @Synopsys2023DSOai]. While these reports show learned methods moving into production workflows, they cannot establish independent functional correctness, guarantee complete physical signoff, or prove a net benefit over a strong conventional alternative.

Together, these examples demonstrate useful pieces of a broader design capability. Learned search and autotuning explore choices; placement and RTL generation produce physical artifacts; tool-using agents invoke real flows; domain adaptation supports selected engineering tasks; and generated designs reach silicon under tightly bounded conditions. The moonshot aims to connect these demonstrated capabilities through current project state and real design tools, all while retaining independent checks robust enough to reject an unsound result. No single existing system has established that complete capability.

Across these systems, each result supports only the specific claim its checks can inspect. Check cost and fidelity, task scope, baseline quality, workflow coverage, and access to supporting artifacts all bound what architects can conclude (@tbl-existing-systems).

| **System** | **What it establishes** | **The telltale limit** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AlphaTensor [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor] | Learned search improved a fifty-year-old matrix-multiplication count for 4 by 4 matrices modulo two | The algebraic construction admits an exact mathematical check, and a single scalar scores it |
| AutoTVM [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM] | Measured search can improve schedules when many candidates run quickly on real hardware | The result covers tensor-program schedules, where failures usually remain safely contained within the tuning run |
| AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment] | A learned policy produces macro placements a production flow accepts | The reward relies on proxy wirelength and congestion, and the matched baseline remains disputed |
| ArchGym [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym] | At equal sample budgets no search algorithm dominates, so the chosen harness and budget ultimately shape the result | Because every candidate is graded by a simulator, the result inherently adopts its fidelity limits |
| Apollo and BOOM-Explorer [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] | Learned design-space exploration can successfully exploit domain-specific evidence | Apollo transfers knowledge across related accelerator spaces to reduce costly target evaluations; BOOM-Explorer uses an open-source core but depends on commercial tools and pays hours per sample |
| VerilogEval and RTLLM [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM] | RTL generation can be measured on shared benchmark tasks | VerilogEval emphasizes functional simulation; RTLLM adds post-synthesis quality metrics; neither reaches physical signoff |
| Chip-Chat and Enlightenment-1 [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat; @ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU] | Generated logic has reached silicon, including a core that successfully boots Linux | One relies on extensive human-guided revision; the other synthesizes a processor from input-output examples with a provable accuracy bound, rather than the full multi-tool system-architecture capability the moonshot poses |
| ChatEDA [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA] | An agent can plan and invoke a real tool flow directly from stated intent | The benchmark checks tool execution and human-rated request fulfillment on 50 ChatEDA-Bench tasks using a simplified OpenROAD wrapper, lacking independent functional correctness or complete signoff |
| ChipNeMo [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo] | Domain adaptation can improve selected internal engineering tasks | The gains remain task-specific, general models stay stronger on certain subtasks, and outsiders cannot reproduce the proprietary evaluation |
| DSO.ai [@Synopsys2023DSOai] | Learned flow-parameter search has reached 100 vendor-reported commercial tapeouts | The evidence standard remains a vendor report, lacking a public methodology or matched baseline |

: **The strength of each result depends on its scope and how it is evaluated.** Exact, inexpensive checks support strong scoped claims, whereas narrow measurements, proxies, weak baselines, and hidden supporting data, methods, or artifacts all limit what architects can conclude. {#tbl-existing-systems tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

This table presents scoped claims rather than a definitive ranking of systems. Shared benchmark tasks make it possible to inspect exactly where each claim stops and where further evidence is required.
